title: Improvised Dixieland tunes and American records bought in Berlin
summary: They improvised on standards like Tiger Rag; later in Berlin a music dealer held every new Red Nichols, Wolverines and Henderson release for him.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: And while you were doing those Dixieland things, that was mostly improvised, or did you have arrangements for that?
Most of them are improvised. They are improvised.
"Tiger Rag," and "Way Down Yonder in New Orleans," and things like that, you know. "I Wish I Could Shimmy Like My Sister Kate"
Sure. Well, by that time, by 1922, there wasn't much jazz on records, though, was there?

No, no. The "Dixieland" was about the only band that really ventured and made real jazz recordings. Then they -- what's his name, this wonderful trumpet player that I like so much, "Red" Nichols. Red Nichols, he started, it was semi-jazz, but I liked him 'cause he had plenty technique and I like that. And Pollard by the Wolverines, Miff Mole, Bix Beiderbecke, they're the ones that really initiated the world in recordings and everything. They initiated the world. I remember at the time, that Red Nichols became popular, I was in Germany,
and I'd go to the music store, and every recording that came out during the month, he would hold for me.
Whether it was Red Nichols or even Fletcher Henderson started at the time.
I got a picture of Fletcher Fletcher Henderson, and Duke Ellington was just starting. But Red Nichols and the Wolverines were top bands, then came Frankie Trumbauer.
And I'd get all the recordings, in this music store, and they'd hold it all for me, wouldn't sell one of the recordings until I came and heard it.
I was at the Barbarina Cabaret in Berlin, at the time.
And that's why my memory of Germany is terrific. Berlin, you can't imagine. One could never have imagined what happened after.
